items.title: Speed limit: max in ideal conditions
items.simple: The speed limit is the fastest you may drive. It is for perfect conditions. You may go slower if you do not hold up traffic. Going faster is against the law.
items.official: A speed limit is the maximum legal speed you can travel on a road under ideal conditions. You may drive slower than the speed limit, as long as you don't impede the normal movement of traffic, but it is illegal to drive any faster.
items.mnemonic: The limit is a ceiling, not a target.

items.title: Must slow for zones and weather
items.simple: Slow down when a school zone or work zone speed limit is on. The law says so. Also slow down when road work or bad weather makes the posted speed unsafe.
items.official: By law you must drive slower where signs indicate a school zone speed limit or work zone speed limit is in effect, and/or if conditions such as road construction or bad weather make the posted speed unsafe.

items.title: Reckless: 20+ over or 85+
items.simple: Going 20 MPH or more over the limit? Police can charge you with reckless driving. Going over 85 MPH? Same thing, no matter what the limit is.
items.official: If you are driving 20 or more miles per hour (MPH) above the speed limit, or over 85 MPH, a law enforcement officer may charge you with reckless driving, regardless of the speed limit.

items.title: Reckless driving is a crime
items.simple: Reckless driving is a crime called a misdemeanor. A judge can fine you, take away your license, or put you in jail. If someone dies while your license is suspended or revoked, it may be a felony.
items.official: It is considered a misdemeanor criminal offense if convicted of reckless driving. The court may require a fine, suspend your driving privilege and/or impose a jail sentence. If the violation results in death and the operator's license was suspended or revoked at the time of the offense, it may be considered a felony.

items.title: Extra $100: 81-85 in 65
items.simple: Picture a 65 MPH zone. Driving 81 to 85 MPH there costs an extra $100 fine. You pay it if you are found guilty.
items.official: You are subject to an additional $100 fine if convicted of driving between 81 and 85 MPH in a 65-MPH zone.

items.title: Radar detectors are illegal
items.simple: You may not use a radar detector in Virginia. It is against the law.
items.official: It is illegal to use radar detectors in Virginia.

items.title: 25 MPH: school, business, homes
items.simple: No speed sign? In school, business and home areas, the top speed is 25 MPH.
items.official: Unless there is a speed limit sign stating otherwise, the maximum speed limit for passenger vehicles and motorcycles is 25 MPH for school, business and residential areas.

items.title: 35 MPH: unpaved roads
items.simple: No speed sign? On an unpaved road, the top speed is 35 MPH.
items.official: Unless there is a speed limit sign stating otherwise, the maximum speed limit for passenger vehicles and motorcycles is 35 MPH for unpaved roads.

items.title: 55 MPH: all other roads
items.simple: No speed sign? On all other roads, the top speed is 55 MPH. Other roads means not school, business, home or unpaved.
items.official: Unless there is a speed limit sign stating otherwise, the maximum speed limit for passenger vehicles and motorcycles is 55 MPH for all other roads.

items.title: School zones may use speed cameras
items.simple: Some school zones use cameras to catch speeders. A sign that says SPEED PHOTO ENFORCED tells you cameras check your speed there.
items.official: Some school zones may have automated photo enforcement, as indicated by signs with the message "Speed Photo Enforced" or similar.

items.title: Three parts of stopping distance
items.simple: Three things add up to your stopping distance. They are perception time, reaction distance and braking distance. Perception time is how long it takes you to spot a danger.
items.official: Three factors determine the distance that it takes to stop your vehicle: perception time, reaction distance and braking distance. Perception time: The time it takes you to recognize a hazard.
items.mnemonic: See it, react, brake: three parts of every stop.

items.title: Reaction distance
items.simple: You spot a problem. Then your foot moves to the brake. The distance your car travels in between is reaction distance.
items.official: Reaction distance: The distance your vehicle travels between the time you recognize a problem and the time you apply the brakes.
items.mnemonic: Reaction distance: before the brake. Braking distance: after.

items.title: Braking distance
items.simple: Braking distance is how far your car moves after you press the brake. Higher speed, worn brakes or tires, and bad pavement make it longer.
items.official: Braking distance: The distance your car travels after you apply the brakes. Braking distance is also affected by how fast your vehicle is traveling, the condition of your brakes and tires, and the pavement condition.
items.mnemonic: Braking distance starts when your foot hits the brake.

items.title: What changes your stopping distance
items.simple: Weather changes how fast you can stop. So does how well you can see and how you feel. Speed, road conditions, how alert you are, and your car's weight matter too.
items.official: Perception time, reaction distance and braking distance are affected by weather, visibility, and your mental and physical condition. Road conditions, speed, driver alertness, and the weight of the vehicle you are driving all change the ability to stop.

items.title: Wet pavement doubles braking
items.simple: Wet pavement can double your braking distance. It can take twice as far to stop in the rain.
items.official: Braking distance is also affected by ... the pavement condition. For example, wet pavement can double your braking distance.

items.title: Never pump antilock brakes
items.simple: Never pump antilock brakes. Learn how your brakes work. Read your owner's manual and practice braking before you drive on the road.
items.official: If your vehicle has antilock brakes, be sure that you understand how they work. Check your vehicle owner's manual and practice braking before you go out on the road. Remember, never pump antilock brakes.

items.title: Keep a space cushion
items.simple: Keep space all around your car. It gives you room to react and avoid a crash. Stay in the middle of your lane. Leave room ahead and behind.
items.official: Space around your vehicle gives you distance to react in emergencies and avoid a crash. Create a space cushion around your vehicle by staying in the middle of your lane. Make sure there is enough room ahead of your vehicle and behind it for other vehicles to pass or stop safely.

items.title: Under 35 MPH: 2 seconds
items.simple: Driving under 35 MPH on a dry road? Stay at least 2 seconds behind the car ahead.
items.official: Following Distance: 2 seconds Under 35 MPH. At these speeds and on dry surfaces, this distance, in seconds, allows the driver to steer and brake out of a problem area.

items.title: 35-45 MPH: 3 seconds
items.simple: Driving 35 to 45 MPH on a dry road? Stay at least 3 seconds behind the car ahead.
items.official: Following Distance: 3 seconds 35-45 MPH. At these speeds and on dry surfaces, this distance, in seconds, allows the driver to steer and brake out of a problem area.

items.title: 46-70 MPH: 4 seconds
items.simple: Driving 46 to 70 MPH on a dry road? Stay at least 4 seconds behind the car ahead. If you speed over 70 MPH, these rules do not work.
items.official: Following Distance: 4 seconds 46-70 MPH. The space cushions above do not work if you're speeding over 70.

items.title: Count seconds from a fixed mark
items.simple: Watch the car ahead pass a fixed object, like a sign or overpass. Count the seconds until you reach it. If you get there too soon, you are too close. Slow down.
items.official: Glance at the vehicle ahead as it passes a fixed object, such as an overpass, sign, fence, corner or other fixed mark. Begin counting the seconds it takes you to reach the same place in the road. If you reach the mark before you have counted off two, three, or four seconds, depending on speed, you're following too closely. Slow down and increase your following distance.

items.title: Add seconds when conditions are bad
items.simple: Add extra seconds to your following distance in bad weather or heavy traffic. Add more on poor pavement, or if your car is in poor shape.
items.official: For bad weather conditions, heavy traffic, poor pavement or if your vehicle is in poor condition, add extra seconds to increase your following distance. Drivers need to change following distance when speed or road conditions change.

items.title: Hand 1/2 second, foot 3/4
items.simple: Your hands react in about half a second. Your foot takes about three-quarters of a second. Being tired, on medicine or distracted slows you down even more.
items.official: Hand response time is close to a half second. Foot response time is normally three-quarters of a second. This does not take into account any delay in perception time as a result of the driver being tired, on medication, distracted, etc.
items.mnemonic: Hand and Half both start with H. Foot is slower: 3/4.

items.title: When to leave extra space
items.simple: Leave extra space behind a big vehicle that blocks your view. Leave extra space behind a motorcycle or bike. Also add space in bad weather, heavy traffic, leaving an expressway, or when tailgated.
items.official: Increase your following distance when driving: behind a large vehicle that blocks your vision; in bad weather or heavy traffic; when exiting an expressway; behind a motorcycle or bicycle; when being tailgated.

items.title: Being tailgated: no sudden braking
items.simple: A tailgater follows you too closely. Do not slam on your brakes. Move to another lane if you can. Or tap your brakes gently and slow down. Then they can pass or back off.
items.official: Tailgating is when one driver follows another too closely. If you find yourself in this situation, do not brake suddenly. If possible, move over to another lane, or gently tap your brakes to flash your brake lights and slow down. This should encourage the tailgater to pass you or slow down. Help the driver behind you by maintaining a safe following distance and a steady speed. Tap your brakes to warn the driver behind you when you plan to slow down or stop.

items.title: Look 20-30 seconds ahead
items.simple: Look far ahead, 20 to 30 seconds. In the city, that is about one block. Keep your eyes moving. Do not stare at one thing or at the middle of the road.
items.official: Searching means looking at the entire scene for anything that might come into your path. As you search the road, avoid staring at one thing. Expert drivers try to focus their eyes 20 to 30 seconds ahead. In the city, that equals approximately one block. Avoid staring at the middle of the road. Scan from side to side.
items.mnemonic: 20 to 30 seconds ahead = about one city block.

items.title: Look left, right, left
items.simple: Before you enter an intersection, look left, then right, then left again. Look left first because cars from the left are closer to you.
items.official: Check from left to right and then left again before entering an intersection. At any intersection, look to the left first, since cars coming from the left will be closer to you. Then look to the right and take one more quick look to the left before you drive through.
items.mnemonic: Left is closest, so left is first and last.

items.title: Look both ways where paths cross
items.simple: Look both ways anywhere cars, people or animals may cross your path. This means intersections, crosswalks, shopping centers, work areas and playgrounds.
items.official: Whenever you reach a place in the road where other cars, people or animals may cross your path, look both ways to be sure it is clear. These include intersections, crosswalks, shopping centers, construction areas and playgrounds.

items.title: Check mirror every 10 seconds
items.simple: Check your rearview mirror often, about every 10 seconds. It shows if someone is coming up too fast or tailgating. Also check before changing lanes, backing up, or slowing down quickly.
items.official: Use your rearview mirror to check the traffic behind you frequently, about every 10 seconds. This will alert you if someone is moving up too quickly or tailgating you. Check the traffic behind you when changing lanes, backing up, slowing down quickly or driving down a long, steep hill.

items.title: Clues a car may pull out
items.simple: Watch for clues that a car may pull into your path. Look for exhaust smoke, brake or back-up lights, and turned wheels. In the country, watch for hidden driveways, curves, hills and slow farm vehicles.
items.official: Search for clues on the road. Look for exhaust smoke, brake or back-up lights and turned wheels on vehicles. Clues like these warn that the vehicles may pull into your path. When driving in rural areas, watch for hidden intersections and driveways, curves, hills and different road conditions.
items.mnemonic: Smoke, lights, wheels: that car may move.

The time it takes to see a hazard
The distance you should follow behind a truck
questions.explain: Braking distance is the distance your car travels after you apply the brakes.

questions.prompt: Braking distance is affected by:
choices: The condition of your brakes and tires
questions.explain: Speed, brakes and tires, and pavement condition all affect braking distance.

questions.prompt: Which of these will make your braking distance longer?
questions.explain: Braking distance is affected by how fast your vehicle is traveling.

questions.prompt: Wet pavement can:
choices: Cut your braking distance in half
Have no effect on braking distance
questions.explain: Wet pavement can double your braking distance.

questions.prompt: Compared to dry pavement, your braking distance on wet pavement can be:
questions.explain: Wet pavement can double your braking distance.

questions.prompt: It is raining. What should you do to allow for a longer braking distance?
choices: Follow closer to see brake lights
Slow down and leave more space
questions.explain: Wet pavement can double braking distance, so slow down and add following distance.

questions.prompt: If your vehicle has antilock brakes, you should:
choices: Pump the brakes quickly in a hard stop
Pump the brakes slowly on wet roads
questions.explain: Never pump antilock brakes.

questions.prompt: Before driving a vehicle with antilock brakes, you should:
choices: Check the owner's manual and practice braking
questions.explain: Check your owner's manual and practice braking so you understand how antilock brakes work.

questions.prompt: Which statement about antilock brakes is correct?
choices: You should pump them on wet pavement
questions.explain: Never pump antilock brakes.

questions.prompt: To create a space cushion around your vehicle, you should:
choices: Stay close to the car ahead
Stay in the middle of your lane
questions.explain: Create a space cushion by staying in the middle of your lane.

questions.prompt: A space cushion around your vehicle:
choices: Is only needed on unpaved roads
Gives you distance to react in emergencies and avoid a crash
Is the same as your blind spot
questions.explain: Space around your vehicle gives you distance to react in emergencies and avoid a crash.

questions.prompt: When driving under 35 MPH on a dry road, you should follow at least ___ behind the vehicle ahead.
questions.explain: Under 35 MPH, the following distance is 2 seconds.

questions.prompt: You are driving 30 MPH on a dry road. The safe following distance is:
questions.explain: Under 35 MPH, use at least 2 seconds following distance.

questions.prompt: At speeds of 35 to 45 MPH on a dry road, your following distance should be:
questions.explain: From 35 to 45 MPH, use a 3-second following distance.

questions.prompt: You are driving 45 MPH on a dry road. How far behind the vehicle ahead should you be?
questions.explain: From 35 to 45 MPH, follow at least 3 seconds behind.

questions.prompt: At speeds of 46 to 70 MPH on a dry road, you should follow at least:
questions.explain: From 46 to 70 MPH, use a 4-second following distance.

questions.prompt: The two-, three- and four-second following distance rules do not work if you are:
questions.explain: The space cushions do not work if you are speeding over 70 MPH.

questions.prompt: Which following distances match these speeds on dry roads?
questions.explain: Use 2 seconds under 35 MPH, 3 seconds at 35-45 MPH and 4 seconds at 46-70 MPH.

questions.prompt: To check your following distance, you should count the seconds it takes you to reach:
choices: A fixed object that the vehicle ahead just passed
questions.explain: Glance at the vehicle ahead as it passes a fixed object, then count the seconds until you reach it.

questions.prompt: You are driving 40 MPH. The car ahead passes a sign. You reach the sign after counting only two seconds. You should:
choices: Slow down and increase your following distance
Move closer to the car ahead
questions.explain: If you reach the mark before counting the right number of seconds, you are too close, so slow down.

questions.prompt: Which can be used as a fixed object when counting following distance?
questions.explain: Use a fixed mark such as an overpass, sign, fence or corner.

questions.prompt: You should add extra seconds to your following distance when:
choices: Your vehicle is in poor condition
questions.explain: Add extra seconds for bad weather, heavy traffic, poor pavement or a vehicle in poor condition.

questions.prompt: When speed or road conditions change, you should:
questions.explain: Drivers need to change following distance when speed or road conditions change.

questions.prompt: The road surface is in poor condition. Your following distance should be:
choices: Longer than the usual 2-, 3- or 4-second rule
The same as on a dry road
questions.explain: For poor pavement, add extra seconds to your following distance.

questions.prompt: Foot response time is normally:
questions.explain: Foot response time is normally three-quarters of a second.

questions.prompt: Hand response time is close to:
questions.explain: Hand response time is close to a half second.

questions.prompt: Which can add delay to your perception time?
questions.explain: Being tired, on medication or distracted can delay perception time.

questions.prompt: You should increase your following distance when driving:
choices: Behind a large vehicle that blocks your vision
questions.explain: Increase following distance behind large vehicles, motorcycles or bicycles, and when exiting an expressway.

questions.prompt: Which situation calls for a larger following distance?
choices: When driving on a dry, empty road
When the car ahead is far away
questions.explain: Increase your following distance when being tailgated.

questions.prompt: Why should you increase your following distance behind a large truck?
choices: It blocks your vision of the road ahead
It is required only at night
questions.explain: Increase following distance behind a large vehicle that blocks your vision.

questions.prompt: If you are being tailgated, you should:
choices: Brake suddenly to warn the driver
Move to another lane if possible, or gently tap your brakes and slow down
questions.explain: Do not brake suddenly; move over or gently tap your brakes and slow down.

questions.prompt: Tailgating is:
choices: Parking too close to a hydrant
questions.explain: Tailgating is when one driver follows another too closely.

questions.prompt: To help the driver behind you, you should:
choices: Keep a steady speed and tap your brakes before slowing down
questions.explain: Keep a safe following distance and steady speed, and tap your brakes before you slow or stop.

questions.prompt: Expert drivers try to focus their eyes:
choices: On the middle of the road
questions.explain: Expert drivers try to focus their eyes 20 to 30 seconds ahead.

questions.prompt: In the city, looking 20 to 30 seconds ahead equals about:
questions.explain: In the city, 20 to 30 seconds ahead is approximately one block.

questions.prompt: When searching the road ahead, you should:
choices: Keep your eyes moving and scan from side to side
Stare at the middle of the road
questions.explain: Avoid staring at one thing; keep your eyes moving and scan from side to side.

questions.prompt: Before entering an intersection, you should look:
choices: Left, then right, then left again
Right, then left, then right again
questions.explain: Check left, then right, then left again before entering an intersection.

questions.prompt: At an intersection, you should look to the left first because:
choices: Cars from the right always yield
Cars coming from the left will be closer to you
questions.explain: Look left first since cars coming from the left will be closer to you.

questions.prompt: You should look both ways to be sure it is clear at:
questions.explain: Look both ways wherever cars, people or animals may cross your path.

questions.prompt: When you reach a place where cars, people or animals may cross your path, you should:
choices: Look both ways to be sure it is clear
questions.explain: Look both ways wherever other cars, people or animals may cross your path.

questions.prompt: You should check your rearview mirror about every:
questions.explain: Check traffic behind you frequently, about every 10 seconds.

questions.prompt: You should check the traffic behind you when:
choices: Backing up or slowing down quickly
Driving down a long, steep hill
questions.explain: Check behind when changing lanes, backing up, slowing quickly or driving down a long, steep hill.

questions.prompt: Checking your rearview mirror often will:
choices: Alert you if someone is moving up too quickly or tailgating
questions.explain: Frequent mirror checks alert you if someone is moving up too quickly or tailgating.

questions.prompt: Which clue warns that a parked vehicle may pull into your path?
questions.explain: Exhaust smoke, brake or back-up lights and turned wheels warn a vehicle may pull into your path.

questions.prompt: You see exhaust smoke coming from a parked car ahead. This means:
choices: The car may pull into your path
The car is broken down for good
You may pass it at any speed
The driver is signaling you to go
questions.explain: Exhaust smoke is a clue that a vehicle may pull into your path.

questions.prompt: When driving in rural areas, you should watch for:
choices: Hidden intersections and driveways, curves and hills
questions.explain: In rural areas, watch for hidden intersections and driveways, curves, hills and different road conditions.
